newsitem.title: USA: Ford hopes Navigator will lure young buyers to Lincoln.
newsitem.headline: Ford hopes Navigator will lure young buyers to Lincoln.

text.p: One automotive industry analyst has dubbed it the "Lincoln Town Truck."

Ford Motor Co. executives prefer to say the new Lincoln Navigator, a full-size sport utility vehicle, represents the future direction of the languishing Lincoln brand by aiming for younger, affluent buyers.

Based on the enormously popular new Ford Expedition, the Navigator weds four-wheel drive mass and utility with luxury car finery. Analysts and dealers who have seen the vehicle say the interior takes its cue from the Town Car -- Lincoln's flagship -- with plush leather seats and walnut trim.
On the outside, the Navigator is distinguished from the Expedition by a different grille that features the Lincoln logo mounted unmistakeably in the middle.
The Navigator is due to go on sale next summer as a 1998 model year vehicle. It will be officially introduced Jan. 7 at the North American Auto Show in Detroit.

Although prices have not been set, they are expected to be in the mid-$40,000 range. That puts Navigator below the base prices of the 1997 Lexus LX 450 and Range Rover, the two high-end sport utilities Ford expects to compete against.
As the first non-car entry in the Lincoln lineup, the Navigator marks a milestone for Ford's traditional domestic luxury brand. And it comes none too soon.
Like General Motors Corp.'s Cadillac division, Lincoln has missed out entirely on the hottest trend to hit the auto market in years: sport utility vehicles.

Meanwhile, import intruders have eaten into Lincoln's share of the luxury car market. The Mercury Mountaineer, an upscale version of the Explorer, helped in 1996. But Lincoln-Mercury dealers are hungry for the Navigator.

"I think there's going to be a tremendous demand for the Lincoln Navigator based on the fact there is not a domestic high-end sport utilty on the market," said Billy Vaughn, general manager of North Park Lincoln-Mercury in San Antonio, Texas.
Aside from the Navigator, Lincoln faces a critical test as the all-important baby boom generation ages: can it shake a stodgy image and entice buyers who came of age driving stylish imports?

Lincoln derives more than half its sales from the mammoth Town Car, a favorite of older men looking for the comfort and size of their living room mounted on four wheels. Through November, total Lincoln sales were off 6.4 percent, after falling almost 16 percent in 1995.

"The issue at the moment is that none of the domestic makes have demonstrated an ability to pull upscale buyers out of Japanese models," said Susan Jacobs, president of industry consultant Jacobs & Associates Inc.
Lincoln-Mercury General Manager Jim O'Connor argues Navigator will put Lincoln on the shopping list of affluent baby boomers who might not have previously considered the domestic luxury make.
Ford plans to continue injecting new products into the line-up. Next August will bring a refreshened Continental. An all-new Town Car will follow in the fourth quarter of 1997.

But how committed is Ford to Lincoln beyond that? Lehman Brothers analyst Joseph Phillippi said some within Ford have questioned the wisdom of propping up Lincoln when it already has Jaguar, a prestige brand that carries valuable cachet with today's import-minded baby boomers.

O'Connor would not comment on future product plans, but he denied that Ford had any plans to abandon the Lincoln brand. Ford Chairman Alex Trotman said recently the company will continue to invest in large luxury cars, even though the luxury car market will remain tough over the next five years.
"I have an open mind about the luxury market," he said.

Industry sources say, however, that Ford in fact is planning to shrink its Lincoln offerings. On the drawing board are plans to drop both the Mark VIII coupe and Continental, a front-wheel drive sedan, sometime after 2000.

That would leave the Town Car, the Navigator and a rear-wheel drive, entry-level luxury car under development, referred to as DEW 98. After that, Ford may let the market decide Lincoln's fate, the sources said.
